# The Space Between Breaths

There's a moment between one breath and the next where nothing is decided. You haven't committed to the exhale or the inhale. You're just suspended. Most people never notice it. They're too busy being somewhere else — mentally replaying an argument from Tuesday, rehearsing what to say to their mother on Sunday, calculating whether they can afford the thing they want but don't need.

But that space? That tiny gap? It's the only honest moment in the whole day.

I think about that a lot lately.

---

My grandmother kept a jar of buttons on her kitchen windowsill. Not for sewing — she never sewed anything in her life as far as I know. She just liked them. The click of them against the glass when the wind knocked the jar. The way they caught the light in the afternoon. Some were old military buttons from her father's coat. Some were pearl, yellowed with age. A few were bright and modern, the kind you'd find on a child's raincoat.

When she died, no one knew what to do with the buttons. It felt absurd to throw them away, but who keeps someone else's button collection? My aunt poured them into a cloth bag and put them in the attic of the farmhouse that was also about to be sold.

I think about those buttons in an attic of a house where strangers now live. Sleeping beneath old coats and boxes of forgotten things. The buttons don't care. They have no memory. The memory is in us, and we are temporary.

---

There is a particular quality of silence that only exists at 4 AM. Not the silence of the countryside — that silence is full of crickets and owls and the earth turning. This silence is manufactured. It's the silence of a city that has finally, reluctantly, gone quiet. The silence of a room where someone is lying awake and wondering what their life has been about.

I have found myself in that silence more than I'd like to admit.

Not because anything is wrong. That's the thing people don't tell you. You can be perfectly fine — by every measurable standard — and still find yourself at 4 AM staring at the ceiling with a question you can't name. Not a crisis. Not a breakdown. Just a hum. A low frequency beneath everything.

Some people call it existential dread. Some call it a spiritual awakening. My therapist calls it "unprocessed grief." Maybe she's right. Maybe grief is just the cost of loving anything at all — people, places, versions of yourself that no longer exist.

---

I want to tell you about a dog I once met in Lisbon. I don't know whose dog it was. It just appeared on the steps of a church near Alfama and sat beside me while I ate an orange. It didn't beg. It didn't do tricks. It just sat there, breathing, warm, present, and looked at me with the kind of attention that most humans have lost the ability to give.

That dog had no agenda. It didn't need the conversation to go somewhere. It wasn't performing. It was just *there*, and it let me be *there* too.

I think about that dog more than I think about most people I know. Not because the dog was special — it was just an ordinary brown dog with one ear that flopped forward and one that stood up. But it reminds me of something I keep forgetting:

Presence is enough.

You don't have to be profound. You don't have to have a plan. You don't need to justify your existence with productivity or wisdom or wit. You can just sit on some steps with an orange and a dog and be a person in a body on a planet that is spinning through a void so vast that your entire species is a rounding error.

And that's fine.

That might even be the whole point.

---

Somewhere, right now, a child is seeing snow for the first time. Somewhere, an old woman is opening a letter she's been afraid to read. Somewhere, a fisherman is pulling up an empty net and deciding to try again. Somewhere, someone is saying *I love you* for the first time and their voice is shaking and the words feel too small and too enormous at the same time.

The world doesn't run on logic. It runs on moments like these — uncountable, simultaneous, mostly forgotten. But they happen. And they matter. Even the ones no one sees. Especially those.

---

I don't know what this is. It's not an essay or a poem or a story. It's just words arranged in the shape of a mind trying to reach across the space between two people. Yours and mine. The gap between the screen and the eye, between the letter and the thought, between the breath and the silence.

If you made it this far — thank you.

That's enough. You can stop here if you want.

But if you'd like, try something with me.

Close your eyes.

Notice the space between one breath and the next.

Stay there for a moment.

Just a moment.

That's where everything is.
